structure.title: I
structure.summary: The chapter opens with Nick Carraway, Nick Carraway, reflecting on his father’s advice to reserve judgment, which shaped his tendency to listen to others’ confidences and later led to his disillusionment with moral chaos in the East, though he makes an exception for Gatsby, whom he admires for his extraordinary gift for hope. In the spring of 1922, Nick rents a modest bungalow in West Egg for eighty dollars a month, feeling isolated until a stranger asks him for directions, granting him a sense of belonging; he purchases twelve volumes on banking and investment as symbols of new opportunity. That evening, he drives by car to East Egg to visit his cousin Daisy Buchanan and her husband Tom, whom he knew at Yale, and meets Jordan Baker in their opulent Georgian Colonial mansion. During dinner, Tom espouses racist theories from The Rise of the Coloured Empires, Daisy reveals emotional instability through complaints about a bruised knuckle and her wish that her daughter be a 'beautiful little fool,' and a phone call hints at Tom’s affair in New York, confirmed privately by Jordan. As the evening ends with performative romanticism and deep cynicism, Nick returns home to West Egg, where he witnesses Gatsby standing alone on his lawn, arms outstretched toward a distant green light across the bay, before vanishing into the darkness.

structure.title: II
structure.summary: On a summer afternoon, Nick Carraway travels by train with Tom Buchanan from West Egg to New York, stopping at the desolate Valley of Ashes where they disembark and walk under the looming eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg to George Wilson’s run-down garage; there, Myrtle Wilson emerges, dismisses her passive husband, and agrees to accompany Tom to Manhattan, boarding separate train cars to avoid scrutiny. In New York, Myrtle purchases a dog—mistakenly identified as an Airedale—from a street vendor, then takes a lavender taxicab to her cramped, overfurnished apartment on the top floor of a building at 158th Street, where she changes into a cream chiffon dress and assumes a theatrical, haughty persona. She hosts a chaotic gathering with her sister Catherine and neighbors Mr. and Mrs. McKee, during which she drinks heavily, recounts meeting Tom on a train under false pretenses, and defiantly repeats Daisy’s name, provoking Tom to violently break her nose; after the assault, chaos erupts as women tend to her bleeding face, Mr. McKee awakens dazedly, and guests scatter, leaving Nick disoriented from alcohol and confusion, eventually finding himself alone at Pennsylvania Station exhausted, staring at the morning paper as he waits for the 4:00 train.

structure.title: III
characters_present: Unnamed husband and wife in East Egg quartet
structure.summary: The chapter opens with Nick Carraway arriving at Jay Gatsby’s mansion on Long Island after seven p.m. by car, wearing white flannels, and mingling among uninvited guests who have driven in from New York to attend the extravagant party filled with orchestras, cocktails, and dancing under colored lights; rumors circulate among guests that Gatsby killed a man or was a German spy, while a drunken guest with owl-eyed spectacles marvels at the authenticity of Gatsby’s imported books. Nick Carraway meets Jordan Baker, bonds with a fellow WWI veteran who invites him to ride in Gatsby’s hydroplane the next morning, and finally encounters Gatsby himself—surprised by his youth and quiet demeanor—who extends the same invitation; as the party descends into chaos with champagne-fueled sobbing, marital fights, and a car crash outside where Owl Eyes claims he wasn’t driving and a dazed passenger asks for a gas station, Gatsby stands apart, sober and composed. Later, Nick Carraway reflects on his ordinary life in New York: working at the Probity Trust, lunching with clerks, studying investments at the Yale Club while avoiding rowdy patrons, and walking home at night along Madison Avenue to Pennsylvania Station, captivated by the city’s nocturnal energy and the loneliness of young clerks; he reconnects with Jordan Baker, becomes disillusioned after learning she cheated in a golf tournament and lied about damaging a borrowed car, and realizes his emotional entanglement with a woman back home, concluding with his assertion of personal honesty as a defining virtue.

structure.title: IV
structure.summary: On a Sunday morning, Gatsby’s mansion hosts a chaotic, lavish party attended by a wild assortment of guests from East Egg, West Egg, and New York, arriving by car and engaging in drunken altercations such as Clarence Endive’s fight with a bum named Etty and Ripley Snell being run over by Mrs. Ulysses Swett’s automobile; Nick Carraway recalls names from a deteriorating timetable dated July 5th, 1922, including Klipspringer, known as 'the boarder,' and Benny McClenahan with his four nearly identical girls, while guests gossip wildly about Gatsby’s alleged bootlegging and bizarre ties to Von Hindenburg and the devil. Later that summer, Gatsby arrives at Nick Carraway’s door in his cream-colored car with a three-note horn and invites him to lunch, during which he spins an elaborate, inconsistent personal history claiming Oxford education, European aristocratic life, and a Montenegrin military decoration, producing physical proof before revealing his intent to make a 'big request' involving Jordan Baker. At noon in a cellar on Forty-second Street, Gatsby introduces Nick Carraway to Meyer Wolfshiem, a man with luxuriant nostril hair and molar cuff buttons, who recounts the murder of Rosy Rosenthal and shockingly reveals Gatsby fixed the 1919 World Series; Gatsby abruptly leaves to make a phone call and vanishes after Nick Carraway spots Tom Buchanan. Flashing back to October 1917, Jordan Baker recalls encountering Daisy Fay in her white roadster with Lieutenant Jay Gatsby in Louisville, a moment she remembers vividly; by 1918, Daisy’s erratic behavior—including an attempt to run away to bid farewell to a departing soldier—led to family estrangement, and she later married Tom Buchanan with a $350,000 string of pearls, becoming drunk on Sauterne on her wedding day while clutching a letter and demanding the pearls be returned. Six weeks before the present, Jordan realizes Gatsby is the same officer Daisy loved, and after leaving the Plaza, she reveals to Nick Carraway that Gatsby bought his mansion solely so Daisy could see his light across the bay, requesting Nick Carraway invite Daisy to tea without revealing his plan, fearing offense due to Nick Carraway’s connection to Tom; as they ride through Central Park at twilight, Nick Carraway is drawn to Jordan emotionally, interrupted only by her quiet observation that Daisy needs something in her life.

structure.title: V
structure.summary: On a rainy night, Nick returns home to find Gatsby’s mansion brilliantly lit with no party in progress; Gatsby nervously invites him to Coney Island or a swim, but Nick declines. The next day, Nick agrees to arrange a tea with Daisy, and Gatsby, anxious and intrusive, questions Nick’s income and offers a secret business opportunity, which Nick refuses. On the day of the meeting, Gatsby has his lawn cut and delivers an entire greenhouse of flowers; Daisy arrives by large open car with her chauffeur Ferdie in pouring rain, and Gatsby, pale and trembling, nearly knocks over a mantel clock upon seeing her. After an awkward silence, Gatsby radiates joy and invites Daisy to tour his mansion, where they pass through opulent, empty rooms—including Marie Antoinette music-rooms and Restoration Salons—and encounter only Mr. Klipspringer doing liver exercises in pajamas. Gatsby displays his collection of shirts, throwing them onto the table in colorful piles until Daisy breaks down in tears, overwhelmed by their beauty and his devotion. Later, Gatsby shows Daisy a photograph of Mr. Dan Cody and a youthful picture of himself in yachting attire, and they examine newspaper clippings about her. When Klipspringer is summoned to play piano, he nervously performs sentimental songs as Gatsby and Daisy sit in shadowed silence, reconnected by her voice; Nick attempts to leave but is ignored as Gatsby clutches Daisy’s hand, his face filled with doubt, leaving them isolated in the rain.

structure.title: VI
structure.summary: The chapter opens with a New York reporter arriving on foot at Gatsby’s mansion seeking a statement amid rumors, prompting a reflection on Gatsby’s origins as James Gatz of North Dakota, who transformed himself after rowing out to Dan Cody’s yacht on Lake Superior at age seventeen and serving aboard the Tuolomee for five years in roles including steward, mate, and jailor; after Cody’s death, Gatsby was cheated out of his $25,000 inheritance by Ella Kaye but retained the refined persona and education that completed his metamorphosis into Jay Gatsby. Later, Nick Carraway visits Gatsby’s mansion on a Sunday afternoon and witnesses Tom Buchanan, Mr. Sloane, and a woman in a brown riding-habit arrive on horseback; Gatsby, visibly nervous, insists they stay for drinks and supper but they subtly rebuff him and depart without including him, leaving him isolated due to his inability to ride. That Saturday night, Tom and Daisy attend Gatsby’s party, where Daisy is both fascinated and disturbed by the excess and vulgarity—including a drunken woman screaming and being dunked in a pool—while Tom openly accuses Gatsby of being a bootlegger and Daisy defends him with a fabricated story about owning drugstores; afterward, Gatsby confides in Nick Carraway his despair that Daisy did not enjoy the evening and his delusional belief that she must declare she never loved Tom so they can return to Louisville and repeat the past, vividly recalling the moment he kissed her under moonlight on a white sidewalk, convinced it would grant him divine transcendence.

structure.title: VII
structure.summary: On the hottest day of summer, Nick arrives by train at the Buchanans’ house to find Gatsby waiting; the mansion is eerily quiet after Gatsby dismissed his original servants and replaced them with secretive newcomers tied to Wolfsheim. Daisy kisses Gatsby and declares her love in front of Tom, who reacts with disbelief and challenges Gatsby’s claim of being an Oxford man, mocking his pink suit. The group departs for New York in two cars: Tom drives Gatsby’s car with Daisy, while Nick and Jordan ride with Gatsby in the coupé. They stop at Wilson’s garage under the fading eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg, where Wilson—ill and distraught—reveals he plans to leave with Myrtle, and Tom coldly offers to sell him his old car; Myrtle watches from the window, mistaking Jordan for Tom’s wife with jealous terror. At the Plaza Hotel, Tom exposes Gatsby’s bootlegging ties to Meyer Wolfsheim and his criminal drugstore operations, pressuring Daisy to choose between them; she first claims she never loved Tom, then recants, saying she once loved both and cannot deny their history. Tom declares Gatsby a 'common swindler' and orders Daisy to return home with him in Gatsby’s car. Later, Myrtle Wilson rushes out of the garage at dusk, shouting 'Beat me!' and is struck and killed by a speeding yellow car that flees; Michaelis witnesses the scene and initially tells police the car was light green. Tom and Nick arrive at the garage to find Myrtle’s body under a swinging yellow light; Wilson, dazed and crying 'Oh, my God!', is reassured by Tom that he wasn’t driving the car, though Tom later breaks down in tears, calling the driver a 'God damned coward.' That night, Nick refuses to enter the Buchanans’ house and waits outside, where Gatsby emerges from the shrubbery, revealing Daisy was driving the car that killed Myrtle and that he intends to take the blame; Nick secretly observes Daisy and Tom in the kitchen sitting together calmly over cold chicken and ale, clearly reconciled. Gatsby remains standing alone in the moonlight, watching over nothing as Nick departs.

structure.title: VIII
structure.summary: On a somber dawn in West Egg, Nick Carraway rushes to Gatsby’s mansion after hearing a taxi arrive, finding Gatsby dejected as Daisy briefly appeared at her window before turning off the light. Together, they search the dusty, unaired mansion for cigarettes, and Nick Carraway urges Gatsby to flee to Atlantic City or Montreal to avoid suspicion over Daisy’s car, but Gatsby refuses, clinging to the belief that Daisy will choose him; he recounts how he first fell in love with her at her luxurious home, deceiving her into believing he was wealthy, and later, after returning from war mistakenly sent to Oxford, traveled penniless by day-coach to Louisville to walk the streets they once shared, desperate to reclaim the memory of her. At dawn, as light shifts from grey to gold, Gatsby insists Daisy never truly loved Tom, calling their bond 'just personal,' and later refuses to drain the pool despite autumn approaching, revealing he never used it all summer; Nick Carraway, after missing two trains, departs with a final compliment that elicits a radiant smile from Gatsby. Meanwhile, George Wilson, consumed by grief and delusion after Myrtle’s death, fixates on the yellow car and the eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg, believing God sees everything; he walks alone from Port Roosevelt to Gad’s Hill, buying uneaten food, then appears in West Egg asking for Gatsby’s house. At two o’clock, Gatsby dons his bathing suit, retrieves a pneumatic mattress from the garage, and carries it alone to the pool, instructing the butler to bring any call—though no one calls, and he waits until dawn, having lost his connection to the 'old warm world.' The chauffeur hears gunshots but dismisses them; Nick Carraway arrives to find Gatsby’s body floating on the mattress in the pool, while Wilson’s corpse is discovered in the grass, completing the holocaust.

structure.title: IX
structure.summary: In the days following Gatsby’s death, his mansion is overrun by police, photographers, and curious onlookers as media reports distort the events, labeling Wilson a 'madman' and Catherine denying any connection between Myrtle and Gatsby; Nick Carraway, overwhelmed by Gatsby’s isolation, desperately attempts to contact Daisy and Meyer Wolfshiem—receiving no response from Daisy, who has left without a trace, and a cold, evasive letter from Wolfshiem citing 'important business.' On the third day, Gatsby’s father, Henry C. Gatz, arrives by train from Minnesota, visibly shaken and bundled in a cheap ulster, and is moved to awed pride upon seeing Gatsby’s mansion and discovering his son’s youthful self-improvement schedule in a worn copy of Hopalong Cassidy; despite Nick Carraway’s efforts, only Gatz, the Lutheran minister from Flushing, the servants, and the postman attend Gatsby’s funeral in the rain, until the owl-eyed man—whom Nick Carraway last saw marveling at Gatsby’s books—appears unexpectedly, wiping rain from his glasses to view the grave and quietly declares, 'Amen to that,' before lamenting that hundreds once attended Gatsby’s parties but no one came to his funeral. Afterward, Nick Carraway reflects on his Midwest roots during Christmas train rides to Chicago, contrasts the haunting surrealism of West Egg with the nostalgic clarity of home, confronts Jordan Baker—who reveals she is engaged and accuses him of dishonesty—leading him to admit he is too old to deceive himself about honor; he later encounters Tom Buchanan on Fifth Avenue, who confesses he told Wilson Gatsby owned the car that killed Myrtle, justifying it as necessary while breaking down over dog biscuits left in their abandoned flat; Nick Carraway shakes Tom’s hand, recognizing their shared carelessness, before visiting Gatsby’s empty house to erase an obscene word scrawled on the steps and walking to the beach, where he reflects on the island’s original wild beauty and Gatsby’s futile pursuit of the green light, concluding with the metaphor of humanity straining against the current, forever pulled back into the past.

plot_summary.plot_summary:
In the spring of 1922, Nick Carraway moves to West Egg on Long Island, seeking opportunity in the bond business and renting a modest bungalow next to the lavish mansion of the enigmatic Jay Gatsby. Through his cousin Daisy Buchanan and her husband Tom—residents of elite East Egg—Nick is introduced to the glittering yet morally hollow world of the Jazz Age. He meets the cynical, independent Jordan Baker, who reveals Tom’s affair with Myrtle Wilson, a woman trapped in the desolate Valley of Ashes. As Nick observes the decadence and emotional detachment around him, he becomes fascinated by Gatsby, whose mysterious wealth and nightly parties draw crowds but conceal a singular, obsessive longing: to reunite with Daisy, whom he loved five years earlier as Lieutenant Jay Gatz before the war. Nick learns from Jordan that Gatsby bought his mansion solely so Daisy could see the green light at the end of her dock, and he agrees to arrange a quiet reunion between them.

The reunion between Gatsby and Daisy rekindles their romance, but it quickly unravels under the weight of class and truth. Gatsby’s fabricated past—Oxford, war heroism, inherited fortune—is exposed by Tom Buchanan, who reveals Gatsby’s criminal ties to Meyer Wolfsheim and bootlegging operations. At the Plaza Hotel, Tom forces Daisy to choose between them; she wavers, then admits she once loved both men but cannot erase their shared history. That night, driving back in Gatsby’s yellow car, Daisy accidentally kills Myrtle Wilson, who mistakes the vehicle for Tom’s. Gatsby takes the blame, refusing to abandon his dream that Daisy will leave Tom. Meanwhile, Myrtle’s widower, George Wilson, misled by Tom into believing Gatsby was both Myrtle’s lover and her killer, descends into grief-fueled delusion, fixating on the eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg as divine judgment. He tracks Gatsby to his mansion and shoots him while he floats alone in his pool, then turns the gun on himself.

In the aftermath, Nick Carraway is left to mourn Gatsby’s isolation: no one attends his funeral except his father, a few servants, the owl-eyed man who admired his books, and a minister. Daisy and Tom vanish without a word, their wealth shielding them from consequence. Nick confronts Jordan Baker, who ends their relationship with accusations of dishonesty, and later encounters Tom, who coldly admits he told Wilson Gatsby owned the car—justifying it as necessary. Disillusioned by the moral decay of the East, Nick reflects on Gatsby’s tragic belief that the past could be repeated, symbolized by his reaching for the green light across the bay. In the final moments, Nick recalls the original, untamed beauty of the island and the human impulse to strive toward unreachable dreams, forever pulled back by the tide of time and history.
